opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different ways it could happen, and they're not mutually exclusive.

The first, and the one people talk about most, is an AI system solving an open problem that mathematicians actually care about, not a contrived benchmark but something that's been sitting in the literature for years, with a proof that's checked and accepted. That would be a moment where the math community says, "Okay, something has fundamentally changed." But I actually don't think that alone is the ChatGPT moment. ChatGPT wasn't a moment because it did one impressive thing. It was a moment because millions of ordinary people could suddenly use it and feel the capability themselves.

So what I really envision is when working mathematicians, and also people outside of math, engineers, physicists, students, start using an AI system as a genuine collaborator in their daily work. You have a conjecture, you sketch an idea, and the system helps you explore it, finds counterexamples, fills in the tedious lemmas, and, critically, gives you something you can trust. That's where formal verification comes in. With languages like Lean, the output isn't just plausible-sounding text. It's a proof a machine can check line by line. A chatbot that sounds confident is very different from a system that's correct with a certificate attached.

The third piece is that math is the foundation for so much else: verifying software, chip design, cryptography, any domain where correctness really matters. So the moment might come not from a mathematician at all, but from someone realizing they can get provably correct reasoning on demand. That's when it stops being a niche research tool and becomes infrastructure.

If I had to put it in one sentence: the ChatGPT moment for AI for math is when trustworthy, verified reasoning becomes something anyone can access, and people start doing math they never could have done alone. We're not there yet, but I think it's closer than most people expect.

r001.rationale: The response mentions applications such as software verification, but does not say the breakthrough would include a coding component.

r002.rationale: It links formal verification to mathematical reasoning by describing collaborative exploration and proofs checked line by line as parts of trustworthy reasoning.

r003.rationale: It describes an AI system people can use and says verified reasoning should be accessible, but does not state that the moment must include a product.

r004.rationale: It describes solving an open problem as one possible milestone, but does not suggest an AlphaGo-like milestone would generally come first.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish Olympiad mathematics from research mathematics as separate milestones.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the ChatGPT moment for math won't look like a model suddenly proving the Riemann Hypothesis. It will look much more ordinary than that, and that's exactly why it will matter.

ChatGPT's moment wasn't about the model being the best at any single task. It was about millions of people realizing, in the same week, that they could talk to the thing and it would be useful. For math, I think the analogous moment is when a working mathematician, or a grad student, or an engineer at a hardware company, sits down with a problem they actually care about, something that isn't in any textbook, and the system produces a proof or a construction that they didn't already know how to do, and it's correct, and it's verified. Not a competition problem with a known answer. A real, open, slightly ugly problem from their own research.

And the key word there is verified. I think formal verification is what makes math different from every other domain. With a chatbot, you read the answer and you sort of decide whether to trust it. With a Lean proof, you don't have to trust anything. The checker either accepts it or it doesn't. So the moment can be sharper for math than it was for language, because there's no ambiguity about whether the thing is right. The question of hallucination just disappears at the level of the final artifact.

So what does that moment actually require? I'd say three things. First, the models need to be able to operate at research length, so hundreds of thousands of lines of formal reasoning, not a one-page olympiad solution. Second, the formalized library needs to be rich enough that the model isn't spending all its time rebuilding undergraduate algebra from scratch. That's a Mathlib problem as much as a model problem, and it's why I think the infrastructure layer is underrated. Third, and this is the part people miss, the interface has to be natural. Mathematicians don't want to write Lean. They want to describe a conjecture in English on a whiteboard and have the system go away and come back with either a proof, a counterexample, or a very precise statement of where it got stuck.

When those three come together, I think you get a cascade. One mathematician posts that an AI closed a lemma they'd been stuck on for two years. Then a hundred do. Then it becomes strange not to use it, the same way it became strange to do research without arXiv. And I suspect it happens first not in the glamorous areas, not number theory, but in places like combinatorics, or in verification of chip designs, where the problems are concrete and the payoff is immediate.

The honest answer on timing is that I think the technical pieces are closer than most mathematicians believe and further than most AI people believe. But I'd be surprised if we're not talking about this as a thing that already happened within a couple of years.

r002.rationale: It links research-level mathematical reasoning to formal verification, presenting a verified proof as the defining outcome of the breakthrough.

r003.rationale: It describes a usable system with a natural interface that takes a conjecture and returns a proof, counterexample, or precise account of where it got stuck.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention an AlphaGo-like milestone or say that one would precede the ChatGPT-like moment.

r005.rationale: It contrasts Olympiad solutions with open research problems, but does not frame them as two separate AlphaGo-like milestones.

astra-6.text:
I think a ChatGPT-like moment for AI for math would be when a mathematician can sit down with a system, explain an idea—even a vague, unfinished one—and have a genuinely productive conversation about it. Could it suggest an approach, find a counterexample, or point out that a seemingly new problem connects to something in another field?

The key is that you need to trust the reasoning. A convincing-looking proof isn’t enough. So I imagine a natural-language interface paired with tools that can check the formal steps, while still leaving room for intuition and exploration.

And perhaps the strongest signal would be that people start using it routinely because it helps them make progress on problems they care about. It wouldn’t just solve a benchmark problem; it would become a useful collaborator in the process of discovering mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a ChatGPT-like moment for AI for math would be when you can sit down with a system and genuinely do mathematics together. You could give it a problem, share a rough intuition, and ask, “Is this approach promising? What am I missing?” It would help you explore examples, spot a flaw in an argument, and suggest a useful next step.

For that to work, it needs to do more than produce a convincing-looking proof. It needs to give us reasoning we can check, recognize when it’s stuck, and distinguish a conjecture from something it has actually established. Formal verification could be a really useful part of that, but the interaction should still feel natural to a mathematician.

So I’d look for the moment when people start using it routinely because it helps them make progress on problems they care about. Solving a famous open problem would be exciting, but helping many more people participate in mathematical discovery could be just as transformative.
